papers.title: Cross-Band Coupling of EEG Infraslow Oscillations during NREM Sleep in Mice.
papers.abstract: The infraslow oscillation (ISO) is a ~ 0.02 Hz rhythmic fluctuation in electroencephalographic (EEG) power during NREM sleep. Prior studies were limited to sigma-band ISO, linked to rhythmic norepinephrine release in mice. Whether ISOs exist in other bands, and how ISOs across bands are coupled, remain unknown. We analyzed cross-band ISO coupling across six frequency bands during NREM using a wild-type (WT) discovery dataset of 122 recordings from 72 mice and WT validation of 7 mice. A transgenic (TG) validation of 6 mice was added to test ISO coupling's robustness to Cre knock-in on the LepR gene (LepR-Cre). Band power time series were filtered to the ISO range of 0.01-0.03 Hz. Cross-band coupling was assessed using Spearman's correlation and phase-locking value (PLV) across all 15 band pairs. ISOs were strongest in alpha, sigma, beta, and theta bands, weak in gamma, and absent in delta. Alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs formed a highly correlated motif with replication in WT and TG (r = 0.61-0.77), while gamma had moderate correlation (r = 0.30-0.42), and delta was uncorrelated (p > 0.05). All band pairs showed significant phase locking with replication (FDR-corrected q < 0.01), with stronger consistency in alpha, sigma, theta, and beta (PLV 0.54-0.71), and weaker consistency involving delta and gamma (PLV 0.12-0.37). EEG ISOs extend beyond the sigma band to alpha, beta, and theta bands, forming a strongly coupled motif that may reflect a fundamental organization principle of sleep microstructures at a minute scale.

ai.summary: Analyzed cross-band coupling of EEG infraslow oscillations (0.01-0.03 Hz) across six frequency bands during NREM sleep in mice, finding that alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs form a strongly correlated and phase-locked motif replicated in wild-type and LepR-Cre transgenic mice, while gamma coupling was moderate and delta was uncorrelated or absent.

papers.title: CADENCE: Open-source software for signal conditioning, feature extraction, visualization and analysis of cardiac optical mapping data.
papers.abstract: Optical mapping is a fundamental tool for cardiac electrophysiology research. Processing of these signals can be non-trivial, requiring multiple pre- and post-processing steps to limit interpretation errors. Existing software packages have features siloed across platforms and require users to combine several packages for in-depth analysis. To address this, we developed CADENCE, an open-source MATLAB-based application combining feature breadth (e.g., SVD denoising, conduction velocity, alternans, annotated rotors) and depth (e.g., 15 independent alternans features across both voltage and calcium modalities) in an end-to-end pipeline including data conversion, signal conditioning, feature extraction, and signal analysis. We demonstrate CADENCE's capabilities across datasets spanning four species (rat, rabbit, pig, and human), three tissue preparations (slices, wedge, and whole heart), and three camera configurations (single, dual, and panoramic). CADENCE was validated against three blinded expert observers (15 hearts) and demonstrated agreement comparable to inter-observer variability (SD ratios 1.07/0.95/0.89 for APD80, activation, CaTD80). Dominant frequency was recovered with a median error of 0.03% across 84 of 88 paced recordings with 1:1 capture. CADENCE's code is publicly available and distributed as a compiled standalone application that the end-user can install and run without a MATLAB license to encourage adoption and standardization across laboratories.

papers.title: REM sleep infraslow rhythms correlate with neuropsychiatric symptom severity.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is commonly divided into phasic and tonic substates based on higher and lower oculomotor activity, respectively. Our previous study described an alternative framework in which REM temporal structure forms a continuum of infraslow rhythms (∼0.01 Hz) across brain and body physiology. We now ask whether these infraslow rhythms vary with neuropsychiatric symptoms, given the long-standing but still inconsistent links between REM and mood- or trauma-related disorders. Using a cross-sectional polysomnographic dataset from male veterans, we examined 59 participants for correlations between REM infraslow rhythms and neuropsychiatric symptom scores, excluding participants with moderate/severe apnea. Oscillations in REM respiratory rate, but not cardiac rate or electroencephalogram beta power, showed higher infraslow frequencies in participants with multiple symptoms, including posttraumatic stress, pain, anxiety, depression, and cognitive difficulties. No significant correlations were found between these symptoms and conventional REM metrics (e.g., REM density, latency and duration). To further examine REM beyond phasic/tonic binarization, we analyzed the timing between oculomotor activity and infraslow oscillations. Eye movements occurred preferentially during periods of high respiratory rate, low beta power and intermediate cardiac rate, with no changes in these temporal relationships across symptom severity. Neuropsychiatric associations with REM infraslow rhythms spanned multiple symptom domains but were physiologically specific, with respiratory rate oscillations representing the strongest readout of symptom burden. Furthermore, REM infraslow cycles across brain and body were differentially aligned with eye movements: a temporal pattern that may serve as a physiological target for neuropsychiatric and mechanistic research. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep has long been studied in relation to neuropsychiatric conditions, but traditional measures of the timing and duration of REM episodes have shown limited consistency for symptom tracking. This study addresses this gap by highlighting a less explored physiological feature within REM episodes: minute-scale, or infraslow, rhythms in respiratory and cardiac rate, as well as oculomotor and brain activity. We report that REM infraslow oscillations, particularly in respiratory rate, occur at higher frequency in participants with worse trauma/mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties. This work is evidence of a possible new REM sleep-based biomarker for multiple diseases.

papers.title: Longitudinal Imaging in a Mouse Model of Focal Cortical Dysplasia Reveals Lesion Expansion and Loss of Pre-Discharge Neuronal Recruitment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective: Focal cortical dysplasia type II (FCD II) is a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy, yet how its lesional circuits behave and change over time in vivo has not been directly observed. Methods: We used a mouse model of FCD II carrying the patient-derived gain-of-function mTORp.L2427P variant introduced by in utero electroporation. Through a chronic cranial window over the lesion, we performed repeated in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of identified dysmorphic neurons, pyramidal cells, and VIP interneurons at defined time points, combined with video-EEG monitoring, to determine seizure status and relate cellular activity to interictal discharges. Results: The lesion was not static in adulthood. Dysplastic cortex expanded progressively. This expansion occurred without the tenascin R/C accumulation reported in human FCD II, and was partly explained by continued somatic growth of dysmorphic neurons. Dysmorphic neurons were generally hypoactive; in seizing mice, both dysmorphic and pyramidal cell activity progressively declined, whereas VIP interneuron activity increased slightly in non-seizing animals. In non-seizing lesional cortex, neurons were reliably recruited immediately before interictal discharges. By late disease stages, pre-discharge recruitment had weakened to the point that lesional layer 2/3 neurons were no more active before discharges than expected by chance. Significance: These findings recast FCD II as a lesion that continues to remodel structurally and functionally throughout adulthood, and does so most markedly in animals with seizures. Growth, a cell-type-specific shift in spontaneous activity, and a progressive loss of the lesion's temporal lead over interictal discharges together suggest that FCD II is a dynamically evolving lesion whose relationship to epileptiform activity changes over time. If the lesion progressively loses its generative role, the window in which removing it can arrest the disease is finite, consistent with clinical evidence favoring earlier surgery.

papers.title: Lifespan Trajectories of Resting State Bipolar EEG Power.
papers.abstract: Normative trajectories of resting state bipolar EEG power over the lifespan were derived from a sample of 5781 participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA), a large multi site study, using 12,906 observations from ages 12 through 70. Trajectories were analyzed using the means, variances, and correlations of data in seven frequency bands (from low theta to high beta) and 24 bipolar channels obtained from 17 electrodes of the 10-20 system. In order to make the study more useful for understanding EEG in the general population, only subjects never having an alcohol use disorder (AUD) diagnosis were included in the study. Bipolar EEG data is derived from the differencing of the signals in adjacent electrodes, either in a lateral (left-right) or sagittal (anterior-posterior) orientation; each difference is called a channel. The power values for the individual observations were calculated by standard Fourier transform based methods. In all cases there are sharp decreases in EEG power from ages 12 to the early 20s after which there are number of divergent patterns: general increases in the beta frequencies, and mixed patterns of increase and subsequent decrease in the theta and alpha frequencies. In these characteristics the lifespan trajectories presented here are similar to the monopolar trajectories described in our previous study Chorlian et al. (2026). Sagittal and lateral bipolar trajectories are similar within each sex and between sexes; the primary difference is the much lower degree of regional difference in the sagittal trajectories as compared to the lateral trajectories. The pairwise inter-frequency (within channel) correlation trajectories between the four theta and alpha frequency bands and the four high alpha and beta frequency bands at each channel show striking sex differences unlike the corresponding monopolar correlations. There are a number of features in the bipolar power trajectories that suggest that the differencing procedure reduces not only local phase synchrony, but also effects of global and regional phase synchrony present in the monopolar data from which the bipolar signals are derived. The inter-frequency correlations at the individual channels are much higher in the bipolar data than the monopolar data, suggesting that global and regional phase synchrony components retained in the monopolar data have greater frequency specificity than the more purely local components in the bipolar data. Further analyses to examine many other features of the data will be undertaken in our subsequent work.

papers.title: A Bayesian functional model with multilevel partition priors for group studies in neuroscience.
papers.abstract: The statistical analysis of group studies in neuroscience is particularly challenging due to the complex spatio-temporal nature of the data, its multiple levels and the inter-individual variability in brain responses. Traditional ANOVA-based studies and linear mixed effects models typically provide only a limited exploration of the dynamics of group brain activity and of the variability in individual responses, potentially leading to overly simplistic conclusions and/or missing more intricate patterns. In this study we propose a novel Bayesian model-based clustering approach for functional data that simultaneously assesses group effects and individual deviations across the main temporal features in the data. To this end, we develop a multilevel partition prior to model the functional scores arising from a functional Principal Components decomposition of neuroscientific recordings. The proposed approach enables a thorough exploration of group differences and individual deviations without compromising on the spatio-temporal nature of the data. Through a simulation study we demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves correct classification in different clustering scenarios under low and high noise levels in the data. Finally, we consider an Electroencephalogram case study involving an object recognition task, where the proposed approach provides new insights into the underlying brain mechanisms generating the data and their variability.

Simulation studies showed correct classification under varying noise levels, and an EEG case study provided new insights into brain mechanisms during object recognition.

papers.title: Phase-dependent EEG decoding of continuous visual stimuli.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations support cognition and perception by organizing information across oscillatory cycles. Although animal studies support this view, evidence in humans is mixed and largely based on transient stimuli. We tested whether alpha oscillations, the dominant human brain rhythm, periodically modulate the strength of visual representations. EEG was recorded while participants viewed long-lasting (2 s) Gabor patches. Using a phase-dependent decoding approach, we quantified stimulus decoding accuracy at specific alpha phases. Decoding performance varied systematically with alpha phase, following a smooth unimodal profile that peaked over occipito-parietal electrodes. These effects emerged well after stimulus onset and generalized to earlier time points, indicating a modulation of visual processing during continuous input. Our findings demonstrate that visual information is represented more accurately at specific alpha phases. This provides strong evidence that sensory processing is shaped by intrinsic brain dynamics and introduces a generalizable decoding pipeline for linking oscillatory phase to neural information processing.

ai.reason: Generalizable EEG decoding method with potential transfer, but visual-phase focus rather than sleep.
ai.summary: Recorded EEG while participants viewed 2-s Gabor patches and applied phase-dependent decoding to test whether alpha phase modulates visual representation strength. Decoding accuracy varied systematically with alpha phase in a unimodal profile peaking over occipito-parietal electrodes, indicating more accurate visual representation at specific alpha phases during continuous input.

papers.title: A Complementary Dual-Branch Receptive Field Network for Cross-Channel-Density Motor Imagery EEG Decoding.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between the brain and external devices, providing a bio-inspired link between humans and artificial systems. However, electroencephalography (EEG)-based motor imagery (MI) decoding continues to pose challenges, due to limited temporal exploitation and insufficient spatio-temporal modeling. To alleviate these limitations, a complementary dual-branch receptive field network (DBRFNet) is proposed for cross-channel-density MI-EEG decoding. Specifically, two complementary branches with distinct temporal receptive fields are designed to capture multi-scale temporal dynamics. Each branch employs a progressive spatio-temporal module integrating temporal, depthwise spatial, and dilated convolutions for modeling short- and long-range temporal dependencies. The features from the two branches are fused using element-wise addition and further encoded for classification. The proposed method is evaluated on three public datasets representing low-, medium-, and high-density EEG configurations. DBRFNet achieves decoding accuracies of 80.48%, 84.37%, and 92.24% under cross-validation analysis, and 87.76%, 80.94%, and 94.64% under hold-out analysis, demonstrating competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component within the proposed architecture. These results indicate that DBRFNet effectively learns discriminative spatio-temporal representations and provides a robust solution for MI-BCI systems.

ai.reason: Transferable cross-channel-density EEG decoding architecture but GPU-heavy deep net with MI-specific focus and limited relevance to sleep staging or animal work.
ai.summary: A complementary dual-branch receptive field network (DBRFNet) was proposed for cross-channel-density motor imagery EEG decoding, capturing multi-scale temporal dynamics through two branches with progressive spatio-temporal modules. DBRFNet achieved decoding accuracies of 80.48%, 84.37%, and 92.24% under cross-validation on three public datasets, demonstrating competitive performance.

papers.title: Transcranial Evoked Potentials are Minimally Influenced by Afferent Feedback From Peripheral Muscle Contraction.
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) investigates cortical reactivity, yet the contribution of sensory feedback from muscle twitches to the recorded signals remains debated. We combined M1 TMS-EEG with electromyography, accelerometry, and peripheral electrical stimulation to dissociate central and peripheral contributions. We compared EEG responses across trials yielding large versus small motor outputs, while peripheral stimulation isolated pure afferent components. Bayesian analysis revealed that larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies uniformly across all time windows-including those too early for peripheral feedback-indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in baseline motor cortex excitability drive both responses. Conversely, isolated muscle contraction produced delayed (> 65 ms), markedly smaller EEG responses with distinct spatiotemporal profiles. We conclude that sensory feedback from muscle twitches contributes minimally to TMS-evoked EEG responses, which instead primarily reflect the baseline excitability state of the stimulated cortex.

Larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies across all time windows including pre-feedback latencies, whereas isolated muscle contraction produced only delayed (>65 ms) small responses, indicating TMS-evoked potentials mainly reflect baseline motor cortex excitability.

papers.title: A Modality-Invariant Measure of Neural Health.
papers.abstract: Quantifying neural health with a single measure remains a major unmet challenge. Here, we report a physiological marker based on the spatial distribution of signal-derived energy correlates in the resting brain. We hypothesize that energy organization in the healthy brain approaches an entropy-maximizing, homeostatically regulated state characterized by five properties: lognormal energy distributions, balanced spatial allocation, statistical independence between regions, low energy variance, and temporal stability. Together, these properties define an energetic profile that the Neural Health Index (NHI) summarizes as a single score, computable from (scalp/intracranial) electroencephalography, magnetoencephalography, or functional magnetic resonance imaging. Across 808 participants spanning neurological, psychiatric, neurodevelopmental, and neurodegenerative disorders, NHI distinguished healthy from clinical populations with sensitivity and specificity exceeding 95% in internal and external validation, scaled with disease severity, tracked pharmacological treatment exposure, and generalized to unseen diagnoses. These findings support NHI as a disease-agnostic, modality-invariant candidate biomarker for disease stratification and treatment monitoring.

papers.title: Spatial Neurophysiological Gradients at High Resolution Differentiate Tumor Types in the Human Cortex at the Tumor-Brain Interface.
papers.abstract: Brain tumors interact bidirectionally with neural circuits, but direct electrophysiological evidence in the human brain across tumor types remains limited. We analyzed intraoperative clinical, mesoscale, and high-density surface electroencephalography recordings from 100 participants undergoing tumor resection, epilepsy surgery, or deep brain stimulation. Population-averaged measures poorly separated diagnoses, whereas spatially resolved aperiodic exponent and high-gamma activity varied with both tumor distance and nearby tumor volume fraction across scales. Gradients differed among IDH-mutant glioma, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and metastases. Connectivity further distinguished infiltrative gliomas: beta coherence across tumor-brain connections was reduced in IDH-mutant tumors (p=0.0006; Kruskal-Wallis; mean coherence: tumor-brain 0.26, tumor-tumor 0.44, brain-brain 0.34), unlike IDH-wildtype tumors or metastases. Physiological abnormalities extended into radiographically normal-appearing brain, indicating tumor-type-dependent physiological signatures that may dynamically map the tumor-brain interface complementing structural imaging, with future possibilities as a spatial biomarker of tumor infiltration and network organization in humans.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation.
papers.abstract: Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Participants had a mean age of 73.8 ± 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome (β: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS (β: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles.
papers.abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations.
papers.abstract: Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ∼50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

papers.title: Vibrotactile transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) during working memory: convergent electrophysiological evidence for cortical efficiency.
papers.abstract: Working memory, the cognitive ability to maintain and manipulate a finite amount of information, is fundamental in reasoning, learning, and decision-making. Working memory erodes in conditions from Alzheimer's disease to stroke to healthy aging. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a promising neuromodulation method for improving working memory. By stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, taVNS is thought to engage ascending arousal systems such as the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system. However, the physiological link between LC-NE system modulation via taVNS and improved working memory remains largely unknown. This mechanistic gap limits the rational optimization of the stimulation protocol and the identification of the cognitive functions and patient populations that are likely to benefit. We test two competing hypotheses for how taVNS may improve working memory: sensory amplification or enhancement of cortical efficiency. The sensory-amplification hypothesis predicts increased cortical responses to stimuli, whereas the cortical-efficiency hypothesis predicts reduced cortical responses. Twenty healthy adults completed N-back working memory tasks during three counterbalanced sessions: baseline, active vibrotactile taVNS (vtaVNS), and sham stimulation, while we simultaneously recorded electroencephalography, electrocardiography, eye-tracking, and behavioral responses. To study the effect of vtaVNS on neuronal activity, we also recruited 20 patients with epilepsy undergoing invasive monitoring. Of these, 19 fully completed the spatial working-memory task. We quantified cortical responses to visual stimuli using event-related potentials (ERPs) in scalp EEG and high-gamma activity in intracranial local field potentials. To examine prediction of the cortical-efficiency hypothesis, we further explored the effect of vtaVNS on distance to criticality and heartbeat-evoked potentials. Active vtaVNS reduced both scalp-recorded visual ERP and high-gamma response in temporal cortices, relative to sham stimulation. Moreover, smaller visual event-related potentials were associated with successful encoding during the most demanding working-memory condition (i.e., 4-back task). Exploratory analyses showed that vtaVNS shifted cortical dynamics closer to criticality. Our results converge on the conclusion that vtaVNS does not uniformly amplify cortical responses to external stimuli. Instead, vtaVNS enhances cortical efficiency, supporting more effective allocation of cognitive resources between exteroceptive and mnemonic processes. These findings provide a framework for predicting when taVNS will be most beneficial and for optimizing stimulation protocols across cognitive and clinical applications. papers.title: Treadmill or Overground? Cognitive-Motor Interference Effects in Healthy Older Individuals.
papers.abstract: Walking is increasingly understood as a cognitively demanding activity requiring the integration of sensory processing, motor control and executive functions. When combined with a concurrent cognitive task (dual-tasking), cognitive-motor interactions may lead to changes in gait, behaviour and neurophysiology. In healthy aging, reduced motor automaticity may result in greater involvement of top-down control, increasing susceptibility to cognitive-motor interference and fall risk, even in the absence of clinical impairment. To explore real-world demands, we compared dual-tasking during outdoor overground walking and during indoor treadmill walking, using behavioural assessment of cognitive task performance, mobile electroencephalography and motion tracking with wearable sensors. Thirty-six older adults performed an auditory Go/No-Go task during both walking conditions and in a seated control condition. Compared to a stationary control condition, results confirmed significant dual-task interference effects during both walking conditions, and this effect was more pronounced during overground walking. The results suggest that overground walking imposes greater demands, leading to increased competition between cognitive and motor processes for shared cognitive resources. The consideration of natural conditions helps to identify the cognitive demands of locomotion.

papers.title: When the heart and the brain meet: Brain-heart interactions in feature integration
papers.abstract: In contemporary Cognitive Neuroscience, increasing attention is devoted to brain-body interactions, as an expanding body of literature suggests that processing the external world may not emerge from the brain in isolation but rather from the coordinated contribution of multiple bodily systems. These interactions have been extensively studied in the context of interoception. However, evidence linking them to visual perception remains scarce. To address this gap, the present study reanalyses a previously published dataset from 25 participants to investigate heart-brain interactions during a visual feature integration task. Participants were required to integrate shape and colour features to identify a target while inhibiting distractor-related information. Cardiac and neural activity were simultaneously recorded, enabling the assessment of the heart rate (HR), heart evoked potentials (HEP), and, albeit seldom reported previously, heart evoked oscillations (HEO). Prestimulus HEP amplitude briefly differed between correctly and incorrectly integrated features. HEO analysis revealed alpha and low beta band modulations before target onset. These effects were absent when the analyses were aligned to external events and exceeded surrogate distributions obtained after disrupting heartbeat EEG alignment, indicating that they depended on cardiac timing rather than on spontaneous prestimulus EEG differences alone. These findings provide preliminary evidence that HEO dynamics are associated with successful perceptual integration and extend previous work on HEPs from stimulus detection to higher-level perceptual processes. More broadly, they suggest that heartbeat-locked neural activity may influence early brain states linked to perceptual outcomes, aligning with theoretical frameworks proposing an active role for bodily signals in perceptual processing.

papers.title: High-dose cerium dioxide nanorods induce behavioral and electroencephalographic abnormalities through 5-HT1B receptor signaling disruption with an evaluation of anpirtoline's therapeutic potential.
papers.abstract: Cerium dioxide nanorods (CeO2 NRs) have drawn extensive research attention in the past few years for their exceptional generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and intrinsic catalytic properties. The two ends of the biological effect show a dose-dependent difference: protection of cells at low doses and damage to cells at high doses. Although the above processes are well documented in other biological contexts, the neurotoxicity induced by acute exposure to CeO2 NRs, as well as its mechanism and possible prevention strategies, have yet to be elucidated. In the present study, we have found that CeO2 NRs at a concentration of 500 μg/mL or higher induced neuronal apoptosis and reduced cell viability in vitro. After intranasal instillation in mice, CeO2 NRs accumulated in the lysosomes and nuclei of neurons in the hippocampus and striatum. There was an increase in these abnormal exploratory behaviors, heightened seizure susceptibility, and altered electroencephalographic (EEG) oscillations. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling further indicated disruption of serotonin (5-HT) metabolism, caused by a downregulation of the 5-HT1B receptor, and thus provided a possible molecular mechanism for the behaviors and EEG abnormalities observed. Considerable changes also occurred in the various serotonergic mediators, neuronal excitability indicators, and inflammatory markers. Pharmacological activation of the 5-HT1B receptor with anpirtoline partially reversed the behaviors and EEG changes induced by CeO2 NRs.

papers.title: Clinical feature-guided targeted genetic testing in early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy: a real-world diagnostic approach in a resource-limited setting.
papers.abstract: In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), access to trio-based whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing is limited, which may delay genetic diagnosis in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE). We used clinical features to guide targeted genetic testing and reviewed the results through multidisciplinary discussion in a Vietnamese pediatric cohort with early-onset DEE and examined its association with treatment decision-making. We prospectively enrolled 51 children aged 0-23 months with early-onset DEE at a tertiary pediatric center in Vietnam between November 2023 and April 2025. Clinical phenotyping included seizure semiology, EEG, and brain MRI. Prior to testing, patients were categorized as hypothesis-driven or non-hypothesis-driven based on clinical and paraclinical features. Targeted sequencing of 108 DEE-associated genes was performed. Variants were reviewed by geneticists and then discussed in multidisciplinary sessions including clinicians. Treatment changes and seizure outcomes were assessed six months after genetic results were disclosed. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in 25 of 51 patients (49%). Diagnostic yield differed between the hypothesis- driven and non-hypothesis-driven groups (93.3% vs 30.6%, p < 0.001). Channelopathy-related genes accounted for the largest proportion of genetic diagnoses. Among genetically diagnosed patients, 20 of 25 had a treatment change accompanied by a ≥ 50% reduction in seizure frequency. In genotype-negative patients with infantile spasms syndrome, phenotype-guided treatment adjustment was followed by effective seizure control in most cases. In this cohort, using clinical features to guide targeted genetic testing, combined with multidisciplinary review of results, was associated with higher diagnostic yield in a hypothesis-driven subgroup and was frequently accompanied by treatment changes linked to improved seizure control.

papers.title: Axonal dysfunction precedes axonal degeneration in a mouse model of progressive parkinsonism.
papers.abstract: Axons of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons "die back" in Parkinson's disease (PD), exhibiting early degeneration relative to cell bodies, a key feature also observed in PD models. A critical step towards understanding the process of axonal neurodegeneration is to determine the physiological properties of dopaminergic axons that are altered during the early stages of cellular dysfunction. Here, we compared the electrophysiology and calcium dynamics of dopaminergic axons in the MitoPark model of PD with age-matched controls. Our experiments show a pronounced reduction in action potential (AP)-evoked calcium signals in MitoPark axons that emerges well before the onset of dopaminergic fiber loss and motor deficits. In addition, calcium imaging and direct axon recording revealed deficits in AP propagation accompanied by alterations in the axonal AP waveform. Therefore, our experimental findings identify the progression of axon-specific physiological deficits that occur long before neurodegeneration, more precisely defining the period that precedes axonal loss.

papers.title: Conductive Polyvinyl Alcohol-Based Hydrogels for Wearable Electronics: Preparation Strategies, Conductivity Enhancement, and Sensing Applications.
papers.abstract: Conductive poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)-based hydrogels combine electrical functionality with the mechanical compliance and biocompatibility required for wearable bioelectronics. However, simultaneously achieving mechanical robustness, stable electrical conductivity, and long-term hydration stability remains challenging. Adopting a performance trade-off perspective focused on wearable sensing, this review examines recent advances in five interconnected areas: (1) fabrication strategies, including freeze-thaw cycling, the Hofmeister effect, mechanical training, and green synthesis routes; (2) conductivity enhancement through electron-conducting pathways (carbon nanofillers, MXene, and conducting polymers), ionic routes (salt and electrolyte doping), and hybrid systems; (3) wearable sensing applications, including physiological monitoring (ECG/EMG/EEG), multimodal biosensing of biofluid analytes, and intelligent sensing devices; (4) environmental resilience and mechanical durability; and (5) regulatory, manufacturing, and clinical translation challenges. Representative studies report tensile strengths exceeding 19 MPa, electrical conductivities above 10 S/m, gauge factors above 10, and self-healing within 1 s; however, these values were obtained for different formulations and under different testing conditions. The review further identifies critical gaps in reproducibility, comparable testing protocols, device-level integration, and scalability, and outlines design considerations for advancing conductive PVA-based hydrogels toward reliable wearable health monitoring systems.

papers.title: Sedation Versus General Anesthesia During Pediatric Electrophysiology Studies: A Paired Comparison.
papers.abstract: Anesthetic strategy may influence tachycardia inducibility during pediatric electrophysiology studies, but direct paired comparisons between sedation and general anesthesia remain limited. This prospective paired-comparison study included 51 pediatric patients aged 5-21 years with supraventricular tachycardia undergoing electrophysiology study under both procedural sedation and general anesthesia during the same session. Procedural sedation consisted of midazolam, fentanyl, and supplemental propofol boluses as needed. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and fentanyl and maintained with sevoflurane. Tachycardia inducibility and electrophysiological parameters were compared between anesthetic conditions using paired analyses. Overall tachycardia inducibility was higher during sedation than during general anesthesia (40/51 [78.4%] vs. 29/51 [56.9%], p = 0.007). No significant differences were observed in atrial effective refractory period, ventricular effective refractory period, atrioventricular nodal Wenckebach point, jump, echo interval, or ventriculoatrial block duration. In patients with atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, inducibility decreased from 84.0% during sedation to 60.0% during general anesthesia (p = 0.109). In the Wolff-Parkinson-White/atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia subgroup, inducibility decreased from 73.1% to 53.8% (p = 0.063), and the accessory pathway effective refractory period, measured by extrastimulus pacing, was prolonged under general anesthesia (p = 0.018). Procedural sedation was associated with greater overall tachycardia inducibility than general anesthesia during pediatric electrophysiology studies. The AVNRT and WPW/AVRT subgroups showed numerically lower inducibility under general anesthesia in the same direction as the overall finding, although these subgroup differences did not reach statistical significance. These findings support individualized anesthetic planning that considers the arrhythmia substrate, the need to preserve inducibility for mapping and post-ablation validation, and patient-specific requirements for procedural stability.

papers.title: Toward Reliable Patient-Specific Aortic Strain Mapping from 4D CTA: Validation, Spectral Structure, and Clinical Potential.
papers.abstract: To develop and validate a framework for spatially resolved ascending aortic strain estimation from 4D computed tomography angiography (CTA) and characterize reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales. We constructed patient-specific aortic strain maps using nnU-Net segmentation, optimized surface remeshing, deformable registration, and mesh-based strain estimation. Finite element (FE)-derived synthetic 4D CT sequences provided controlled reference deformations for registration validation. Strain reliability was characterized across segmentation sources and Laplace-Beltrami (LB) spectral scales. Associations with diameter, aortic height index (AHI), and age were assessed. Registration-derived median strain showed minimal bias relative to FE-reference strain for observer-derived (0.0013) and nnU-Net-derived meshes (0.0056). Median strain exhibited low bias and narrow 95% limits of agreement (LoA) across segmentation sources (interobserver: bias = -0.0045, LoA [-0.0490, 0.0399]; nnU-Net versus observer: bias = -0.0052, LoA [-0.0340, 0.0237]). Differences were greater for 95th-percentile strain, particularly in the interobserver comparison. LB spectral analysis showed preferential preservation of low-frequency strain organization, with k = 5 reconstructions reducing segmentation-related disagreement by 52-56%. The 95th-percentile areal strain was inversely associated with maximum ascending aortic diameter (r = -0.493, p = 0.005), AHI (r = -0.488, p = 0.005), and age (r = -0.479, p = 0.006). Three high-grade AR cases showed heterogeneous regional strain patterns. This framework reproducibly estimates ascending aortic strain from 4D CTA, characterizes its reliability across segmentation sources and spatial scales, and demonstrates its potential for noninvasive assessment of patient-specific aortic mechanics.

papers.title: Lead Exposure During Differentiation Perturbs Electrophysiological Function in iPSC-Derived Cardiomyocytes in a Cell Line-Dependent Manner.
papers.abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure is strongly associated with cardiovascular diseases, but the effects of developmental Pb exposure on the electrophysiological properties of human cardiomyocytes have not yet been investigated. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cardiomyocytes, we investigated the effects of human-relevant Pb exposure during ventricular cardiomyocyte differentiation on action potential properties and calcium dynamics in differentiated myocytes. We exposed 2 iPSC lines, from 1 male and 1 female donor, to Pb (0.5 µM or 5 µM) or control during only the first 8 days of differentiation, prior to functional maturation. Differentiation was carried out using an established protocol involving temporal modulation of Wnt signaling, followed by purification and maturation of contractile myocytes. We measured action potential properties and calcium dynamics using fluorescent dyes and optical mapping. We hypothesized that Pb exposure would adversely affect cardiomyocyte function, with effects persisting after cessation of exposure. In keeping with this hypothesis, we found significant Pb-induced changes in calcium (Ca) transients and action potential dynamics that were concentration and cell line specific and persisted well after exposure had ended. In the female cell line, beat frequency significantly increased with Pb exposure for both action potentials and Ca transients, while in the male cell line, beat frequency significantly decreased with Pb exposure for action potentials and increased for Ca transients. For voltage measurements, we observed significantly increased arrythmias with Pb exposure in both cell lines. Significant changes in repolarization and recovery time (for voltage and Ca, respectively) were present with Pb exposure in both cell lines. Gene expression of Ca transporters/channels and K channels were not affected, suggesting that persistent effects of Pb exposure on cardiomyocyte electrophysiology may occur through post-translational mechanisms. Overall, this study paves the way for future work to examine how exposure to Pb impacts long-term cardiac function through developmental programming. All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.

papers.title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate.
papers.abstract: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ∼1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC₅₀=2.22 μM), with comparable potency against Ca v 3.1 (IC 50 =1.63 µM). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

papers.title: Antibody-Related Mechanisms in Ocular Diseases: Autoimmunity, Malignancy, and Therapeutic Targeting.
papers.abstract: Antibodies in ocular disease have heterogeneous biological meanings: they may act as direct pathogenic effectors, systemic diagnostic biomarkers, indicators of B-cell clonality, or therapeutic agents. This distinction is particularly important in the eye, where immune privilege and the blood-ocular barrier restrict tissue access, whereas inflammation may permit entry of immunoglobulins, complement, and immune cells or support local humoral responses. This narrative review integrates antibody and B-cell biology across autoimmune and paraneoplastic retinopathies, aquaporin-4-immunoglobulin G-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, ocular myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, systemic autoimmune and fibroinflammatory disorders with ocular involvement, and B-cell malignancies including vitreoretinal and ocular adnexal lymphoma. We distinguish the evidence for direct antibody pathogenicity from disease association and emphasize that a positive result is interpretable only in relation to the ocular phenotype, assay platform, titer, specimen compartment, and orthogonal confirmation. Serum testing, ocular-fluid analysis, electrophysiology, multimodal imaging, cytology, histopathology, immunophenotyping, immunoglobulin clonality, and molecular testing have complementary roles. Therapeutic strategies include B-cell or B-lineage depletion, complement inhibition, cytokine- or receptor-directed monoclonal antibodies, insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor blockade, and emerging FcRn- or plasma-cell-directed approaches; however, regulatory status and ocular-specific evidence vary substantially among diseases. A mechanistically stratified framework may reduce overdiagnosis, improve recognition of malignant masquerade syndromes, and support more precise selection of targeted therapy.

papers.title: 14-3-3 Enables β-Adrenergic Regulation of the Cardiac Sodium Channel at the Intercalated Disc
papers.abstract: Background: Beta-Adrenergic stimulation enables the heart to adapt electrical activity to increased physiological demand. Although the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 is essential for impulse propagation, the mechanisms underlying its acute beta-adrenergic regulation, particularly within distinct cardiomyocyte membrane domains, remain poorly understood. We investigated whether the phosphorylation-sensitive adaptor protein 14-3-3 mediates this regulation. Methods and Results: Using automated patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs), we found that isoproterenol rapidly increased sodium current (INa) and promoted channel activation at more hyperpolarized potentials, whereas PKA inhibition reduced INa. Disruption of 14-3-3 function abolished these responses without substantially altering basal sodium current or Nav1.5 surface expression. Macropatch recordings from ventricular myocytes revealed that isoproterenol preferentially enhanced INa at the intercalated disc, an effect prevented by 14-3-3 inhibition. Proximity ligation assays further demonstrated increased Nav1.5/14-3-3 proximity following beta-adrenergic stimulation. Systematic mutagenesis identified S460 in the Nav1.5 DI-DII linker as a critical determinant of acute PKA-dependent regulation. Molecular modeling predicted that S460 phosphorylation stabilizes the Nav1.5/14-3-3 interaction. In CRISPR-engineered S460A iPSC-CMs, acute beta-adrenergic regulation of INa was abolished, whereas the isoproterenol-induced increase in conduction velocity was significantly attenuated. Computational simulations further predicted that enhanced intercalated-disc sodium current supports increased conduction velocity across varying conditions of electrical coupling and pacing rate. Conclusions: Our findings identify 14-3-3 and S460 as critical determinants of spatially selective beta-adrenergic regulation of Nav1.5 at the cardiac intercalated disc. This mechanism provides a molecular link between sympathetic signaling and cardiac sodium current regulation, supporting the concept that localized enhancement of Nav1.5 function contributes to the adaptation of cardiac conduction during increased sympathetic demand.

papers.title: Asymmetric assembly underlies activation mechanism of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels.
papers.abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are principal effectors of inhibitory GPCR signaling. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule imaging, electrophysiology and molecular dynamics to define the architecture and activation of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels. GIRK1/2 preferentially assembles as an asymmetric heterotetramer containing one GIRK1 and three GIRK2 subunits. Three PIP₂ molecules bound to GIRK2 promote partial cytoplasmic-domain docking, whereas engagement of a fourth PIP₂ by GIRK1 completes docking and opens the helix bundle crossing gate. GIRK1 also remodels the electrostatic environment beneath the selectivity filter, where its E141 and D173 residues create a permeation module that enhances K⁺ conduction. The GIRK1-selective activator ML297 binds at the GIRK1-GIRK2 interface and controls both permeation and gating. These findings establish how asymmetric assembly couples sequential lipid-dependent gating to efficient K⁺ permeation and GIRK1-dependent pharmacological activation.

papers.title: Activation pathway of the human voltage-gated proton channel.
papers.abstract: Many protein functions are coupled to proton transfer, yet the underlying mechanisms remain extremely difficult to resolve by experiment or conventional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The human voltage-gated proton channel H V 1 (hH V 1) plays key roles in human physiology, but how voltage and pH together drive its activation remains unresolved. Experimental structures of hH V 1 are limited to the X-ray structure of a mouse chimera and NMR models of a truncated hH V 1, both representing an intermediate resting state. Here we determine the activation pathway of hH V 1, together with structural models of its resting and activated states, using an approach that integrates all-atom continuous constant-pH MD (CpHMD), weighted-ensemble (WE) path sampling, and AlphaFold modeling. Starting from an AlphaFold model selected for consistency with resting-state experimental data, over 100 µ s of simulations reveal a mechanism in which transmembrane voltage, assisted by proton titration, drives an outward displacement of the transmembrane segment S4 accompanied by a one-click reorganization of countercharge pairings. These events are enabled by a delicately balanced electrostatic landscape and pH-modulated breathing motions in the resting state that prime the channel for protonation-state switches upon voltage sensing, a principle that may underlie other proton-coupled voltage-gating processes. The simulations also uncover lipid-binding sites at which POPG selectively stabilizes the S4-up conformation, whereas POPE can stabilize either state. These predictions are validated against extensive electrophysiology, mutagenesis data, and new smFRET experiments, which support the one-click S4 displacement and the lipid effects. WE-CpHMD, implemented in the AMBER package, is applicable to other proton-coupled processes that remain elusive.
